definition.text: Policy is a decision point every consequential action passes through before it runs: a structured request -- who is acting, what they want to do, on what, under which run context -- goes in, and a deterministic allow or deny plus the rule that decided it comes out, evaluated before anything is spent or done, never after. This repo's own target contract states the timing directly: "Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend."

evidence.quote: Refusal is deterministic and happens before execution, not after spend

standards.role: governs the decision engine's language and query API behind this card's interface: rules as declarative Rego data, evaluated by OPA, answering a JSON decision request with a JSON decision.
standards.covers: does not standardize the wire contract between an enforcement point and a decision point -- a gap the AuthZEN Authorization API (published as a Standards Track specification in March 2026, no directory under standards/ in this repo) was built to close by deliberately avoiding the decision method itself; and it does not cover authentication, budget accounting, or the safety/compliance rule content this card's own sub-line also names -- those are separate concerns.

evidence.text: To make an authorization decision, an application queries OPA with JSON input, and OPA evaluates the input against the specified policies to return an access decision in JSON.

evidence.quote: To make an authorization decision, an application queries OPA with JSON input, and OPA evaluates the input against the specified policies to return an access decision in JSON.

tools.name: Open Policy Agent (OPA) / Rego
tools.note: the engine this repo names as its adapter today for the Policy capability.

tools.name: Cedar
tools.note: the named second engine behind the same decision API; reported substantially faster than Rego on equivalent scenarios, and restricted-by-design for static analysis. Not in use here.

evidence.text: Proposed: Cedar has been reported as substantially faster than Rego and OpenFGA on equivalent authorization scenarios, but after X-litmus-b-017's text was corrected to the article's actual content (a discussion of AuthZEN's design choice to standardize only the communication protocol, naming Cedar only as one of several mature policy languages with no benchmark figures), the specific 28.7x-35.2x / 42.8x-80.8x performance numbers are no longer supported by any fetched record and are carried here as an unsourced note pending re-verification.

landscape.text: The decision engine's own market is unsettled even as its interface converges: OPA's core creators, including Styra's CTO, were hired by Apple in August 2025, and Styra's own commercial products were released as open source with the company's own future left uncertain, though OPA itself remains an open-source, CNCF-governed project. "Apple has acquired the core developers behind the Open Policy Agent (OPA), including Styra CTO Tim Hinrichs... Despite this talent acquisition, the OPA project itself remains unaffected. The open source code continues to be governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)... In a significant boost for the open source ecosystem, Styra's commercial OPA offerings are also being released as open source... The future of Styra as a company remains uncertain." (a correction from an earlier draft of this card, whose citation to CNCF's own bare project page for this same claim was found not to contain any of it -- see gaps). Cedar is a live, faster, more restricted alternative, and the property that actually settled in this window is not a winning engine but a language-neutral wire contract between the enforcement point and the decision point (AuthZEN, published March 2026), so an engine is now a swappable adapter rather than the interface itself.

evidence.quote: Apple has acquired the core developers behind the Open Policy Agent (OPA), including Styra CTO Tim Hinrichs, in a move that strengthens its global cloud services authorisation infrastructure. Apple, already a major OPA user, will now integrate the expertise of the inventors directly into its operations.

Given that OPA (Rego), Cedar, Topaz, and others already have mature policy languages, standardizing only the interface that connects PDPs to PEPs is more practical than also standardizing a policy language.

usage.text: A caller does not embed permission logic in the code that acts: it sends one decision request -- the actor, the action, the resource, and the run context -- to a decision point reached the same way from every enforcement point, and gets back an allow or deny plus the deciding rule before the action runs, never after. The most-cited production shape for an agent runtime puts this call in front of the tool gateway itself: "the gateway calls OPA before invoking the tool, and OPA answers in well under a millisecond."

gaps.what: This card's own sub-line, 'Guardrails · authN/Z, budgets, safety, compliance', bundles four concerns this repo names as belonging elsewhere. AuthN/Z is cap-identity's own contract -- "Every action names an actor, including delegated agent actors. Delegation chains are explicit" (F-b4-03) -- and reappears verbatim at rail.1 Security ('Identity, authN/Z, secrets, isolation'). Budgets is concern-budget's contract -- "Every unit of work carries a ceiling. Exceeding it terminates the unit, not the platform" (F-b4-02) -- and reappears at rail.4 Cost Management ('Budgets, quotas, showback, unit economics'). Compliance also reappears at rail.2 Governance ('Policy, compliance, audit, access controls'), which names 'Policy' a second time too. Only 'safety' and the deterministic-decision mechanism itself are uniquely this card's.
gaps.why_it_matters: A card whose sub-line lists four concerns two of which are already owned by named capabilities (cap-identity, concern-budget) and all four of which reappear on other rail cards is not describing one seam; code written against this card risks re-deciding authN/Z or budget inside the policy engine instead of calling the capability that already owns it, and the Policy/Governance boundary is drawn twice with no stated rule for which wins.
gaps.research_query: does any harness or example call cap-identity's or concern-budget's own interface from inside the policy decision path, or does the policy adapter decide those questions itself

gaps.what: Measured directly for this card: `bash harness/policy/test.sh` returns 'passed 45, failed 0' -- the swap proof, resume-after-pause check and deliberate breakage all hold. But PASS.md's own current-state table records the opposite about production wiring: "Policy in the gate path | Conformance checks exist; not wired into the enforcement path" (F-a6-04, status defined_not_running).
gaps.why_it_matters: The two facts are compatible once separated -- the harness proves the interface and its adapters can swap, not that a live enforcement point calls it today -- but a flat 'built' status collapses that distinction, and the record on file for the live wiring is older than the harness result and may be stale either way.
gaps.research_query: has PASS.md A6's 'not wired into the enforcement path' row been re-checked since the policy harness gate went green, or does a real caller still bypass the decision point

gaps.what: The identity input a decision request depends on is itself unbuilt: "No identity field anywhere in the system" (F-a6-05, status defined_not_running).
gaps.why_it_matters: A DecisionRequest's subject/actor is exactly the field cap-identity is supposed to supply; if identity is not running, the authN/Z half of this card's own bundled sub-line has no real actor to decide about, which is the concrete mechanism behind gap 1's overlap.
gaps.research_query: what value does the live policy adapter put in the decision request's subject field today, given F-a6-05

gaps.what: This card's landscape claim about Apple's August 2025 acqui-hire of OPA's creators and Styra's wind-down was previously cited to https://www.cncf.io/projects/open-policy-agent-opa/, CNCF's bare project page -- a page whose entire text is one acceptance/incubating/graduated-date sentence plus case-study links. It never mentions Apple, Styra, or an acquisition at all; a byte-for-byte re-check found zero occurrences of either name. The citation has been repaired to a genuinely fetched news article (opensourceforu.com), and the claim itself was narrowed: that source confirms Apple hired OPA's core developers (including Styra's CTO) and that Styra's commercial products were open-sourced, but it states Styra's own future as a company is merely 'uncertain,' not that the company 'has since wound down' as the prior (unsupported) wording asserted.
gaps.why_it_matters: The original citation was a fabrication risk of the worst kind for a landscape claim: a real-sounding, specific event attached to a URL that supports none of it. The corrected wording is more conservative than the original and should not be strengthened back to 'wound down' without a source that actually says so.
gaps.research_query: has Styra's corporate status (dissolved, dormant, or continuing under a different form) been confirmed by a primary source (e.g. Styra's own site, a SEC/corporate filing, or a follow-up report) since August 2025
